summary:
India Fire Calendar is a free web app that turns NASA's split MODIS and VIIRS fire-hotspot records into one consistent daily record for India (2000–2026), shown as a burning-activity calendar for any area you select.

When VIIRS joined in 2012, detection counts jumped because the sensor got sharper, not because fires increased. We express every day as what one VIIRS S-NPP satellite would detect, using ratios learned where satellites overlap plus a machine-learning model for the daily shape. Tested on years it never saw, it cut Punjab & Haryana's bias from +22 % to +3 % and daily error by 28–43 %.

Draw an area or pick a preset to see historical fire patterns, unusual conditions and critical periods (when the season usually starts, peaks and ends), then download or share it. Responders, scientists and land managers get an honest baseline: every number shows its data source and typical error.

Punjab & Haryana's 2026 stubble season so far is 93 % below normal and 16 % below last year in VIIRS detections. But our sensor comparison flags that MODIS Aqua, now passing later in the afternoon, sees more fires than VIIRS, consistent with burning shifting later in the day. Read the drop with caution.
details:
In short: India Fire Calendar turns 26 years of NASA fire hotspots from four satellites into one consistent daily record, and shows it as a burning-activity calendar for any area in India. Tested on years it never saw, it cut the Punjab & Haryana bias from +22 % to +3 %. Its sensor-comparison view also surfaced a real caveat on the recent decline in stubble burning (see "Example").

THE PROBLEM

MODIS (2000–) sees fires at about 1 km; VIIRS (2012–) sees them at 375 m and detects about 5× more by day. Add up raw detections and 2012 looks like an explosion of fire; in fact the instrument changed. Without a consistent baseline, nobody can say whether this season is unusual for their district.

WHAT IT DOES

A free web app with no login. It works on a phone.

- Pick an area: draw one anywhere in India, or choose a preset. The four presets are four burning regimes: Punjab & Haryana crop stubble, Northeast jhum, Central India forests and Uttarakhand forests.

- Burning-activity calendar: one row per year (2000–2026), one square per day. No coverage is shown as unknown, never as zero.

- Historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, critical periods: the typical day and range; anomalies against long-term, last-5-years and last-year baselines; when each season usually starts, peaks and ends, and whether this year is early or late, above or below normal.

- Now & next: the last 30 days against typical, and when the next critical period usually begins. It's based on past patterns, not a forecast.

- Where and which sensor: fire-density and anomaly maps, and each satellite's raw counts next to the harmonized value.

- Honest by design: every year and day shows which satellites it rests on and its typical error.

- Share: CSV, titled charts, and a link to any view.

HOW IT WORKS

- Data: NASA FIRMS active fires (MODIS C6.1; VIIRS 375 m S-NPP and NOAA-20), Nov 2000 – Nov 2026. Cleaned and counted per 0.1° cell per day.

- One unit: every day is expressed as what one VIIRS S-NPP satellite would detect. From 2012, S-NPP is used as is, with NOAA-20 filling its gaps at about 1:1. Before 2012, MODIS is converted with ratios learned where both flew (2012–2019), separately for every 2° area × month × day/night. A gradient-boosted model (LightGBM) then shapes the days within each month; monthly totals stay those of the ratios.

- Validated on four years the method never saw (2013, 2017, 2021, 2025), against a single constant ratio: Punjab & Haryana bias +22 % → +3 %; India daily correlation 0.87 → 0.91; Punjab & Haryana monthly error 26 % → 16 %; the hybrid cuts daily error a further 28–43 %, confirmed on four fresh years.

- Pass bar written down in advance: one criterion was missed (Punjab & Haryana bias +9.7 % on the fresh years, likely MODIS orbit drift in recent years), and we report it. We also tested averaging 5 models to steady the day-to-day shape; it missed our pre-set stability bar, so we kept the simpler version.

- Reproducible: one command rebuilds every published file bit for bit from the raw FIRMS files.

EXAMPLE: PUNJAB & HARYANA STUBBLE BURNING

- Oct–Nov detections fell from 97,882 (2016) to 6,870 (2025).

- The 2026 season so far is 4,733: −93 % against the long-term typical, −82 % against the last five years, and −16 % against last year. The app shows all three, because the answer depends on the baseline.

- In 2025 the paddy-stubble season fell to 9 % of typical while the wheat season stayed near normal (119 %), so the decline measured by VIIRS is specific to paddy burning.

- Our sensor-comparison view surfaced a caveat. Since 2022, MODIS Aqua's detections here moved from about 13:15 to 15:30 local solar time, while both VIIRS satellites stayed near 13:10, and Aqua now sees more fires than VIIRS. This is consistent with burning shifting later in the afternoon, after the VIIRS pass. It doesn't prove it (Aqua's view angle also changed). So the drop should be read with caution, and the app says so next to the numbers.

BENEFITS, AND WHO IT IS FOR

- Responders: is this season above normal or late, and when does the critical period usually start here?

- Scientists: a consistent 26-year daily record with per-day accuracy and a CSV that opens directly in pandas or R.

- Land managers: compare a district with its own history; export a titled chart for a briefing.

- Testing: simulated user testing, with an AI role-playing 8 user types and no access to our code, over 4 rounds plus a final smoke check. The roles were a district disaster officer, an air-quality scientist, a forest officer, a Delhi air-quality forecaster, an agriculture analyst, a journalist, a Space Apps judge on a phone and a Central India forest official. We fixed what it found between rounds. Round 2 flagged MODIS Aqua rising while VIIRS fell, which prompted the sensor-comparison check behind the Aqua finding. This was AI role-play, not real users; testing with real responders is a next step.

LIMITS

- Detections are hotspots at overpass time, not burned area; clouds hide fires, and late-afternoon burning is under-detected.

- Pre-2012 values are estimates (MODIS-era daily error 22–38 %; before July 2002, lower confidence).

- 0.1° (about 11 km) is the finest grid at which 1 km MODIS and 375 m VIIRS can be compared fairly; it suits area-level calendars, not field-level mapping. Presets are boxes or outlines, not official boundaries.

WHAT'S CREATIVE ABOUT IT

- One currency for four satellites, learned per area, month and day/night.

- A hybrid: simple validated ratios set the totals, and machine learning only shapes the days.

- Uncertainty is shown, not hidden. The sensor comparison works as a scientific instrument, and it found the Aqua drift.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Users' real questions ("is this unusual? when do we get ready?") come first; validation comes before claims.

- Access and cost: free, phone-friendly, static files on free hosting.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

A free, honest baseline for fire and air-quality teams, then:

- harmonize fire intensity (FRP)

- link to burned area

- add NOAA-21

- a higher-resolution VIIRS-only layer (375 m points, 2012 onwards) for field-cluster mapping, kept separate from the harmonized 0.1° record

- The pipeline is a template: point it at any country's FIRMS data (one setting) and it rebuilds the harmonized record there, re-learning that region's conversion ratios and re-running the same validation; India's ratios and accuracy figures are not reused.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

- Pipeline: Python (Polars, PyArrow, LightGBM, scikit-learn, Matplotlib).

- Web app: JavaScript, React and Vite, Leaflet with an OpenStreetMap basemap; hosted on Firebase.

- AI assistance: code, analysis and documentation were produced with Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant, directed and reviewed by Ashish Das.

- Code (MIT): https://github.com/tw-Zent/india-fire-calendar. Derived data CC BY 4.0.

- How to cite: Das, A. (2026). India Fire Calendar: harmonized MODIS/VIIRS active-fire record for India, v1.3.1. NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. https://github.com/tw-Zent/india-fire-calendar

- Full method, validation tables and limits are on the app's Methods page: https://nasa-space-app-2026.web.app
